questions.q: Why did Wrenhaven's checkout-api fail to start in Central US during the drill, even though the database and routing had already failed over successfully?
options: Front Door failed to route any traffic to Central US at all
The database replica in Central US had never actually been created
It could not reach the single Key Vault instance it depended on for secrets, which lived only in the unreachable primary region
Checkout-api had no code deployed in Central US
questions.explain: Compute, database, and cache were all genuinely redundant -- but every service in both regions depended on one unreplicated Key Vault instance in the primary region.

questions.q: What made this scenario a genuine case of a hidden single point of failure, rather than just an incomplete architecture?
options: The application-layer architecture was actually redundant at every layer a typical dependency check covers -- the gap was one layer below it, in shared supporting infrastructure
Wrenhaven never built any redundancy at all before this incident
The chaos experiment from Lesson 30 had already predicted this exact failure
Front Door itself was the single point of failure in this scenario
questions.explain: Compute, database, and cache redundancy were all real and correctly built; the single point of failure was a shared dependency underneath that layer, not a missing one within it.

questions.q: Why did Chapter 4's original dependency map fail to catch this gap?
options: It recorded that checkout-api depended on Key Vault but never asked whether that dependency was itself region-redundant, or just assumed to be
The dependency map was never built for this project at all
Dependency maps are only required for database dependencies, not secrets stores
The dependency map incorrectly listed Key Vault as redundant when it wasn't
questions.explain: The map recorded a true but incomplete edge -- it stopped at "depends on," without asking whether the dependency's own redundancy matched the service calling it.

questions.q: According to this case study, what other kinds of shared infrastructure commonly hide the exact same failure mode as the unreplicated Key Vault?
options: Container registries and build pipelines
Load balancer health check configurations
Monitoring dashboards and alerting rules
A shared DNS provider or a single identity provider tenant that both "redundant" regions call to authenticate
questions.explain: The lesson calls out DNS and identity providers as common disguises for the same pattern: application redundancy sitting on top of one unredundant shared dependency.

questions.q: What is the actual lesson behind the fix, beyond deploying a second Key Vault instance in Central US?
options: That Key Vault should never be used for secrets management in a multi-region architecture
That re-running the dependency-mapping exercise against every existing edge -- asking if the other end is itself redundant -- is what actually closes this class of gap, not just fixing one vault
That game days should be run only once per year to avoid team fatigue
That chaos experiments should replace game days entirely going forward
questions.explain: Fixing one vault doesn't prevent the next hidden single point of failure; re-asking the redundancy question against every dependency edge is the real, repeatable fix.
